claim: Global synchronization of vasomotion induced by oscillating visual stimuli was identified in the mouse brain.
source: The presence of global synchronization of vasomotion induced by oscillating visual stimuli was identified in the mouse brain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Endogenous autofluorescence can be used to quantify vasomotion by measuring the vessel 'shadow'.
source: Endogenous autofluorescence was used and the vessel 'shadow' was quantified to evaluate the magnitude of the frequency-locked vasomotion.
evidence: The abstract describes the methodological approach using autofluorescence for vasomotion measurement.

claim: Vasomotion can be quantified in non-transgenic wild-type mice using wide-field macro-zoom microscopy.
source: This method allows vasomotion to be easily quantified in non-transgenic wild-type mice using either the wide-field macro-zoom microscopy or the deep-brain fiber photometry methods.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this methodological capability.

claim: Vasomotion can be quantified in non-transgenic wild-type mice using deep-brain fiber photometry methods.
source: This method allows vasomotion to be easily quantified in non-transgenic wild-type mice using either the wide-field macro-zoom microscopy or the deep-brain fiber photometry methods.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this methodological capability.

claim: Vertical stripes horizontally oscillating at 0.25 Hz induce oscillatory vasomotion locked to the temporal frequency of visual stimulation.
source: Vertical stripes horizontally oscillating at a low temporal frequency (0.25 Hz) were presented to the awake mouse, and oscillatory vasomotion locked to the temporal frequency of the visual stimulation was induced not only in the primary visual cortex but across a wide surface area of the cortex and the cerebellum.
evidence: The abstract describes the experimental stimulus and resulting vasomotion response.

claim: Visually induced vasomotion occurs not only in the primary visual cortex but across a wide surface area of the cortex and cerebellum.
source: Vertical stripes horizontally oscillating at a low temporal frequency (0.25 Hz) were presented to the awake mouse, and oscillatory vasomotion locked to the temporal frequency of the visual stimulation was induced not only in the primary visual cortex but across a wide surface area of the cortex and the cerebellum.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the spatial extent of the vasomotion response.

claim: Visually induced vasomotion adapts to a wide range of stimulation parameters.
source: The visually induced vasomotion adapted to a wide range of stimulation parameters.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly.

claim: Repeated trials of visual stimulus presentations result in plastic entrainment of vasomotion.
source: Repeated trials of the visual stimulus presentations resulted in the plastic entrainment of vasomotion.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes this plasticity phenomenon.

claim: Horizontally oscillating visual stimulus induces horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR).
source: Horizontally oscillating visual stimulus is known to induce horizontal optokinetic response (HOKR).
evidence: The abstract states this as established knowledge.

claim: The amplitude of HOKR eye movement increases with repeated training sessions.
source: The amplitude of the eye movement is known to increase with repeated training sessions, and the flocculus region of the cerebellum is known to be essential for this learning to occur.
evidence: The abstract presents this as established knowledge about HOKR.

claim: The flocculus region of the cerebellum is essential for HOKR learning to occur.
source: The amplitude of the eye movement is known to increase with repeated training sessions, and the flocculus region of the cerebellum is known to be essential for this learning to occur.
evidence: The abstract presents this as established knowledge about HOKR.

claim: There is a strong correlation between average HOKR performance gain and vasomotion entrainment magnitude in the cerebellar flocculus.
source: Here, we show a strong correlation between the average HOKR performance gain and the vasomotion entrainment magnitude in the cerebellar flocculus.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this correlation as a finding of the study.

claim: Plasticity of vasomotion and neuronal circuits occur in parallel.
source: Therefore, the plasticity of vasomotion and neuronal circuits appeared to occur in parallel.
evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the correlation findings.

claim: Efficient energy delivery by entrained vasomotion may contribute to meeting energy demand for increased coordinated neuronal activity and neuronal circuit reorganization.
source: Efficient energy delivery by the entrained vasomotion may contribute to meeting the energy demand for increased coordinated neuronal activity and the subsequent neuronal circuit reorganization.
evidence: The abstract proposes this as a potential functional significance of the findings.

claim: Energy consumption in the brain is super-efficient compared to modern computers.
source: Energy consumption in the brain is considered to be super-efficient compared to that of modern computers (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Howarth et al., 2012; Sokoloff, 1960).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple sources supporting this claim.

claim: Energy (oxygen and glucose) is delivered to the brain via blood vessels.
source: Energy (i.e., oxygen and glucose) is delivered to the brain via the blood vessels.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Vasodilation and vasoconstriction spontaneously occur at seconds time scale (~0.1 Hz).
source: Vasodilation and vasoconstriction spontaneously occurring at seconds time scale (~0.1 Hz) have been reported (Davis et al., 2008; Fujii et al., 1990; Hundley et al., 1988; Jones, 1853).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple sources reporting this phenomenon.

claim: Spontaneous vasomotion was first described in the vein of the bat wing.
source: Such spontaneous 'vasomotion' without any apparent external stimuli was first described in the vein of the bat wing (Jones, 1853) and was subsequently observed mainly in the arteries and arterioles of numerous species (Fujii et al., 1990; Hundley et al., 1988).
evidence: The introduction cites Jones, 1853 as the first description.

claim: In mice, the temporal pattern of spontaneous vasomotion is two orders of magnitude different from the frequency of heartbeat (~10 Hz).
source: In mice, the temporal pattern of such spontaneous vasomotion is two orders of magnitude different from the frequency of heartbeat (~10 Hz; Ho et al., 2011; Kramer et al., 1993).
evidence: The introduction cites sources supporting this frequency difference.

claim: Vasomotion should be considered distinct from pulsation due to heartbeat.
source: Therefore, vasomotion should be considered distinct from pulsation due to heartbeat.
evidence: This is stated as a logical conclusion from the frequency difference.

claim: Slow vasomotion is likely beneficial for efficient delivery of blood in small vessels.
source: The slow vasomotion is likely beneficial for the efficient delivery of blood in small vessels as has been indicated by mathematical modeling (Meyer et al., 2002).
evidence: The introduction cites mathematical modeling supporting this claim.

claim: Vasomotion has been suggested to facilitate the clearance of unwanted substances such as Aβ.
source: Vasomotion has also been suggested to facilitate the clearance of unwanted substances such as Aβ (Aldea et al., 2019; van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites sources suggesting this function.

claim: Vasomotion can be affected by neurovascular coupling mechanisms.
source: Although vasomotion can spontaneously occur on its own without the presentation of any apparent external stimuli, it can also be affected by neurovascular coupling mechanisms (Rivadulla et al., 2011; van Veluw et al., 2020; Villringer and Dirnagl, 1995).
evidence: The introduction cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claim: Neuronal firing triggers the release of vasodilator signals from neurons and/or astrocytes.
source: Neuronal firing triggers the release of vasodilator signals from neurons and/or astrocytes (Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction cites a source supporting this mechanism.

claim: Blood vessels dilate through the relaxation of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and pericytes in response to vasodilator signals.
source: In response to these signals, the blood vessels dilate through the relaxation of the smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and the pericytes (Davis et al., 2008; Peppiatt et al., 2006).
evidence: The introduction cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claim: Functional hyperemia is the vasodilation response to neural activity caused by sensory stimulation.
source: The vasodilation response to the neural activity caused by the sensory stimulation is termed 'functional hyperemia' (Nippert et al., 2018; Stickland et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: The introduction defines functional hyperemia with citations.

claim: Functional MRI signals largely reflect signals created by changes in blood flow.
source: The functional MRI signals largely reflect signals created by the changes in the blood flow (Glover, 2011; Ogawa et al., 1990).
evidence: The introduction cites sources supporting this relationship.

claim: Functional hyperemia confined to a sensory-specific region has been previously reported.
source: Functional hyperemia confined to a sensory-specific region has been previously reported (van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a source reporting this phenomenon.

claim: Visually induced vasomotion became perfectly frequency-locked to the presented stimuli with repeated training.
source: Our unique observation was that the visually induced vasomotion developed with repeated training and became perfectly frequency-locked to the presented stimuli.
evidence: The introduction describes this as a unique finding of the study.

claim: Plastic entrainment of vasomotion occurred globally throughout the whole cortex and was not limited to the visual cortex.
source: Such plastic entrainment occurred globally throughout the whole cortex, and it was not limited to the visual cortex.
evidence: The introduction describes this as a finding of the study.

claim: Repeated exposure to horizontally oscillating visual pattern results in increased amplitude of HOKR eye movement.
source: Repeated exposure to such a pattern results in an increased amplitude of the HOKR eye movement (Ito, 1982; Kanaya et al., 2023; Waespe and Henn, 1977).
evidence: The introduction cites sources supporting this HOKR learning phenomenon.

claim: Neuronal circuit plasticity required for HOKR learning takes place in the flocculus region of the cerebellum.
source: Neuronal circuit plasticity required for the HOKR learning takes place in the flocculus region of the cerebellum.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: A concomitant increase in HOKR performance and magnitude of frequency-locked vasomotion was observed.
source: A concomitant increase in the HOKR performance and the magnitude of the frequency-locked vasomotion was observed.
evidence: The introduction describes this as a finding of the study.

claim: Plastic change of vasomotion dynamics may support and interact with neuronal circuit plasticity.
source: These results suggest the plastic change of vasomotion dynamics may support and interact with the neuronal circuit plasticity.
evidence: The introduction proposes this interpretation of the findings.

claim: Blood vessels in the brain can change their diameter through the actions of SMCs and pericytes.
source: Blood vessels in the brain can change their diameter through the actions of the SMCs and the pericytes (Davis et al., 2008; Peppiatt et al., 2006).
evidence: The Results section cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claim: Spontaneous vasomotion was observed in unanesthetized head-restrained awake mice.
source: Here, we observed spontaneous vasomotion in vivo in unanesthetized head-restrained awake mice.
evidence: The Results section describes the experimental observation.

claim: Anesthesia or creation of an invasive cranial window could potentially perturb naturally occurring vasomotion.
source: Anesthesia or the creation of an invasive cranial window could potentially perturb naturally occurring vasomotion.
evidence: The Results section states this as a methodological consideration.

claim: Blood vessels on the surface of the brain could be visualized through an intact skull when coated with transparent resin, but images were inevitably blurred.
source: Blood vessels on the surface of the brain could be visualized through an intact skull when the skull is coated with a transparent resin; however, the images were inevitably blurred.
evidence: The Results section describes this methodological observation.

claim: Spontaneous vasodilation/vasoconstriction oscillations were observed through thinned-skull cranial window.
source: Therefore, in initial experiments, the thinned-skull cranial window (Drew et al., 2010; Morii et al., 1986) was created (Figure 1A). Spontaneous vasodilation/vasoconstriction oscillations were observed.
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The full width at 10% maximum of TexasRed fluorescence was used as an indication of vessel diameter.
source: Therefore, the TexasRed fluorescence intensity profile perpendicular to the axis of blood flow in the vessel was measured, and the full width at 10% maximum of the TexasRed fluorescence was taken as an indication of vessel diameter (Figure 1B and C; 45.7 ± 9.6 [S.D.] µm, n = 5 vessels observations; see validation of the use of full width at 10% maximum for vessel diameter estimation in the 'Materials and methods' section).
evidence: The Results section describes the measurement method with reference to Figure 1B and C.

claim: The diameter of selected vessels suggests that mostly pial arteries or arterioles were observed in stereomicroscope studies.
source: The diameter of the selected vessels suggests that mostly the pial arteries or the arterioles were observed for the stereomicroscope studies.
evidence: The Results section infers the vessel type from diameter measurements.

claim: Vessel diameter and peak TexasRed fluorescence correlated well.
source: Therefore, the peak TexasRed fluorescence within the blood vessels was also quantified. The vessel diameter and the peak TexasRed fluorescence correlated well; that is, a larger vessel diameter resulted in a higher peak fluorescence (Figure 1F).
evidence: The Results section describes the correlation shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Spontaneous vasodilation events occurred with near-instantaneous rise and apparent exponential decay.
source: Spontaneous vasodilation events were observed with the near-instantaneous rise and an apparent exponential decay.
evidence: The Results section describes the temporal characteristics of vasodilation events.

claim: Vasodilation events occurred relatively periodically with an inter-event interval of 15.8 ± 4.8 s.
source: The vasodilation events occurred relatively periodically (15.8 ± 4.8 [S.D.] s), were relatively fixed in amplitude (10.4 ± 3.7 [S.D.]%), and the half-width of duration was also relatively constant (1.6 ± 0.4 [S.D.] s; n = 9 sessions from five vessels observations).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data on vasodilation event characteristics.

claim: Creation of thinned skull may perturb naturally occurring vasomotion as heat or vibration from drilling can influence brain tissue surface.
source: It is possible that even the creation of the thinned skull may perturb the naturally occurring vasomotion as heat or vibration created by the drilling was reported to influence the surface of brain tissue (Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020).
evidence: The Results section cites a source supporting this concern.

claim: Blood vessels could be well resolved through intact skull coated with transparent resin without using a two-photon microscope.
source: Thus, the blood vessels were observed through the intact skull coated with a transparent resin. The blood vessels could be surprisingly well resolved with this method without the use of a two-photon microscope; however, compared to the thin skull observation, the boundary between the vessel and the brain parenchyma was more vague (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The Results section describes the imaging capability with reference to Figure 2A-C.

claim: TexasRed fluorescence intensity fluctuations better represent vessel volume changes than vessel diameter estimates in intact skull imaging.
source: As the intensity profile was shallow with intact skull imaging, the full width at 10% maximum of the profile appeared to be less reliable as an indicator of vessel diameter and measurements of the TexasRed intensity fluctuations would better represent the vessel volume changes stemming from vasomotion.
evidence: The Results section concludes this based on the imaging characteristics.

claim: Intense autofluorescence from brain tissue could be detected with ~430 nm excitation and ~540 nm emission.
source: During these macro-zoom microscopy recordings, we noticed that an intense autofluorescence from the brain tissue could be detected with ~430 nm excitation and ~540 nm emission.
evidence: The Results section describes this observation.

claim: Most autofluorescence appeared to be coming from the brain parenchyma, with the inside of blood vessels mostly devoid of this autofluorescence.
source: Most of the autofluorescence appeared to be coming from the brain parenchyma. The inside of the blood vessels was mostly devoid of this autofluorescence.
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial distribution of autofluorescence.

claim: TexasRed and autofluorescence fluorescence traces nearly completely mirrored each other.
source: Dynamic fluorescence intensity changes of the TexasRed and autofluorescence were simultaneously observed (Figure 2G). The two fluorescence traces nearly completely mirrored each other (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: The Results section describes the relationship shown in Figures 2G-I.

claim: Inverted autofluorescence dynamics reflect vasomotion dynamics.
source: Therefore, the inverted autofluorescence dynamics would also reflect the vasomotion dynamics.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the mirroring observation.

claim: Several cycles of oscillatory fluctuations at low frequencies (0.1–0.5 Hz) were spontaneously observed in 500-µm-diameter ROI.
source: To simulate the situation using images from the brain surface, a 500-µm-diameter circular region of interest (ROI) was drawn and the average TexasRed fluorescence dynamics were plotted (Figure 2J and K). As apparent from the spectrogram of the trace, several cycles of oscillatory fluctuations at low frequencies (0.1–0.5 Hz) were spontaneously observed.
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: The frequency of oscillatory fluctuation within a cluster was not strictly fixed at a constant value.
source: The frequency of the oscillatory fluctuation within a cluster was not strictly fixed at a constant value.
evidence: The Results section describes the variability in oscillation frequency.

claim: Spontaneous behaviors such as whisking, twitching, or struggling could cause functional hyperemia resulting in interruption of periodic oscillations.
source: It is possible that spontaneous vasomotion detected in our system through the intact skull in awake in vivo mice was less periodic because spontaneous behaviors such as whisking, twitching, or struggling could cause functional hyperemia resulting in the interruption of apparent periodic oscillations.
evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation for the observed variability.

claim: Horizontally oscillating visual stimuli induce involuntary eye movement where the line of sight follows the stimuli in head-fixed mice.
source: Horizontally oscillating visual stimuli are known to induce involuntary eye movement and the line of sight follows the stimuli in head-fixed mice.
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge.

claim: Repeated presentation of HOKR stimuli induces a gradual increase in the amplitude of eye movement.
source: Repeated presentation of the stimuli also induces a gradual increase in the amplitude of the eye movement and the small flocculus region of the cerebellum has been shown to be responsible for this learning (Aziz et al., 2014; Ito, 1982).
evidence: The Results section cites sources supporting this learning phenomenon.

claim: In Novice mice, TexasRed signals fluctuated with non-fixed low frequencies consisting mainly of <0.3 Hz.
source: In response to the first visual training session, fixed frequency oscillation of the TexasRed intensity at the primary visual cortex (V1) was not observed. TexasRed signals in these 'Novice' mice, fluctuated with non-fixed low frequencies which consisted mainly of <0.3 Hz (Figure 3C, left).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In Trained mice, Fourier transform of TexasRed signal at V1 revealed a clear sharp peak at 0.25 Hz.
source: After a couple of more training sessions and just before the fourth training session, TexasRed was administered again. In these 'Trained' mice, the TexasRed signal in the cortex fluctuated periodically. Fourier transform of the TexasRed signal at V1 during the 15 min training session revealed a clear sharp peak in the amplitude spectrum at 0.25 Hz, which was not observed in the Novice mice (Figure 3C, middle).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Second and third harmonic signals were sometimes observed in the frequency spectrum.
source: We also noticed that, although the amplitudes were often much smaller, second and third harmonic signals were sometimes observed.
evidence: The Results section describes this observation.

claim: Second harmonic signal could be explained if visually induced vasomotion reacts to both directions of oscillating stimuli.
source: The second harmonic signal could be explained if visually induced vasomotion reacts to both directions of oscillating stimuli.
evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation.

claim: In Expert mice, the 0.25 Hz fluctuation in TexasRed signal becomes visible in raw traces.
source: With further repeated training sessions (8–11 training sessions), the TexasRed signal fluctuation further becomes more strongly tuned to the frequency of the visual stimuli ('Expert', Figure 3C, right). In this Expert mouse, the 0.25 Hz fluctuation in the TexasRed signal becomes visible even in the raw traces.
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In Expert mice, as soon as visual stimulus started, a sharp rise in 0.25 Hz frequency amplitude increased.
source: Before the visual stimulus, the amplitude at 0.25 Hz was negligible; however, as soon as the visual stimulus started, a sharp rise in 0.25 Hz frequency amplitude increased.
evidence: The Results section describes the temporal dynamics in Expert mice.

claim: Vasomotion amplitude locked to visual stimulus frequency quickly dissipated upon cessation of visual stimulus.
source: The amplitude gradually declined but stayed significant until the cessation of the visual stimulus and the vasomotion amplitude locked to the visual stimulus frequency quickly dissipated (Figure 3D and E, left panel).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Averaged PR0.25 in the whole brain surface ROI gradually increased as training progressed.
source: Averaged PR0.25 in the whole brain surface ROI gradually increased as the training progressed (Figure 3H).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3H.

claim: PR0.25 in V1 and V2 was high but not particularly high compared to S1 or Cb or anywhere else that could be observed.
source: The location of V1, secondary visual cortex (V2), primary sensory cortex (S1), and the cerebellum (Cb) was roughly identified based on the coordinates of the mouse brain atlas by referring to the bregma and lambda locations. PR0.25 in V1 and V2 was high but not particularly high compared to S1 or Cb or, in fact, anywhere else that could be observed.
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial distribution of PR0.25.

claim: The phase of 0.25 Hz signal fluctuation was nearly synchronized across different ROIs.
source: An example of the actual TexasRed signal fluctuation trace in various ROI is shown in Figure 3I. The 0.25 Hz signal fluctuations were apparent in all ROI and, in addition, the phase of the signal fluctuation was also nearly synchronized (n = 5 animals; data not shown).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Frequency and phase-locked vasomotion are not restricted to the visual-related area.
source: These data show that frequency and phase-locked vasomotion are not restricted to the visual-related area, and enhancement and entrainment of vasomotion are observed widely throughout the surface of the brain.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the spatial distribution data.

claim: If TexasRed had to be injected before every training session, the mouse did not learn HOKR very well.
source: However, we found that, if TexasRed had to be injected before every training session, the mouse did not learn very well.
evidence: The Results section describes this observation.

claim: Stress induced by tail vein injection may interfere with the HOKR learning process.
source: It is possible that the stress induced by the tail vein injection interfered with the learning process.
evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation.

claim: Already acquired HOKR learning with multiple training sessions does not get lost with stressful injection.
source: However, as demonstrated below, an already acquired HOKR learning with multiple training sessions does not get lost with the stressful injection.
evidence: The Results section states this observation.

claim: Blood vessels appear as dark 'shadows' in the dYFP fluorescence image.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, the blood vessels are devoid of the fluorescence from the YFP expressed in astrocytes, and thus the blood vessels appear as dark regions in the images.
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dilation or constriction would appear as a decrease and increase in the fluorescence signal of YFP.
source: Therefore, dilation or constriction would appear as a decrease and increase in the fluorescence signal of the YFP.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the shadow imaging principle.

claim: Both TexasRed and dYFP signals fluctuated with 0.25 Hz temporal frequency directly matching the visual stimulus, but mirrored in direction of change.
source: Both TexasRed and dYFP signals simultaneously monitored with fiber photometry fluctuated with the 0.25 Hz temporal frequency directly matching the visual stimulus, but mirrored in the direction of change (Figure 4D).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Not only in the cortex but also deep in the cerebellum, vasomotion can be induced with visual stimulation.
source: The TexasRed signal oscillations were locked to the temporal frequency of the visual stimulus. This shows that, not only in the cortex but also deep in the cerebellum, vasomotion can be induced with visual stimulation.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the fiber photometry data.

claim: The average phase shift of dYFP relative to TexasRed was 184.4° ± 17.6°.
source: The average phase shift of dYFP relative to TexasRed was 184.4° ± 17.6° (S.D.) (Figure 4G; n = 13 segments with 5 min durations each), indicating that these signals were nearly completely inverted.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: dYFP signals can be used for assessing vasomotion dynamics.
source: This shows that dYFP signals can be used for assessing the vasomotion dynamics.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the phase analysis.

claim: Robust HOKR learning could not be reliably induced in Mlc1-tTA::tetO-YCnano50 transgenic mice for unknown reasons.
source: Unfortunately, robust HOKR learning could not be reliably induced in this line of transgenic mice for unknown reasons.
evidence: The Results section states this observation.

claim: When signals collected using 400 µm diameter fiber photometry were analyzed, TexasRed fluorescence and autofluorescence did not mirror completely and a significant shift in phase was observed (246.9° ± 49.9°).
source: However, when the signals collected using the 400 µm diameter fiber photometry were analyzed, TexasRed fluorescence and autofluorescence did not mirror completely and a significant shift in the phase was observed (Figure 4H–J; 246.9° ± 49.9° [S.D.], n = 28 segments).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data shown in Figure 4H-J.

claim: The phase shift in autofluorescence could be due to the additive effect of 'shadow' imaging and concentration fluctuation of autofluorescent metabolite.
source: The phase shift in the autofluorescence could be due to the additive effect of 'shadow' imaging of the vessel and to the concentration fluctuation of the autofluorescent metabolite.
evidence: The Results section proposes this explanation.

claim: The amplitude of 0.25 Hz temporal frequency component of both TexasRed and autofluorescence signals increased with training.
source: The TexasRed fluorescence and the autofluorescence signals are shown for the initial sessions (Novice, Figure 4K) and after several training sessions (Trained). The amplitude of the 0.25 Hz temporal frequency component of both the TexasRed and the autofluorescence signals increased with training (Figure 4K and L).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 4K and L.

claim: A strong correlation between PR0.25 of autofluorescence and that of TexasRed was found.
source: PR0.25 of autofluorescence was plotted against that of the TexasRed for multiple training sessions and a strong correlation between these two parameters was found (Figure 4M).
evidence: The Results section describes the correlation shown in Figure 4M.

claim: PR0.25 of autofluorescence reflects the amplitude of vasomotion locked to the visual stimulation cycle.
source: Therefore, although the autofluorescence dynamics result from the fluctuations reflecting the 'shadow' of vasomotion and an unknown fluctuation source, the PR0.25 apparently reflects the amplitude of the vasomotion locked to the visual stimulation cycle.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the correlation data.

claim: Autofluorescence fluctuations followed changes in temporal frequency of visual stimulation from 0.15 Hz to 0.50 Hz.
source: First, the temporal frequency was changed from 0.25 Hz to 0.15 Hz or 0.50 Hz while keeping other parameters fixed. Interestingly, the autofluorescence fluctuations followed the changes in the temporal frequency, and a clear sharp amplitude at the frequency locked to the presented visual stimulation was evident in the amplitude spectrum in all conditions (Figure 5A).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant difference in peak ratio was found for temporal frequencies ranging from 0.15 to 0.50 Hz.
source: The peak ratio of the autofluorescence was examined for temporal frequency ranging from 0.15 to 0.50 Hz and normalized to that of 0.25 Hz (PR0.25; Figure 5D, left panel). No significant difference was found, showing that vasomotion can lock to any temporal frequency within the range examined.
evidence: The Results section describes statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Vasomotion can lock to any temporal frequency within the range examined (0.15-0.50 Hz).
source: No significant difference was found, showing that vasomotion can lock to any temporal frequency within the range examined.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the statistical analysis.

claim: Visually induced vasomotion quickly adapted to any new frequency tested and the reversibility of adaptation was confirmed.
source: The visually induced vasomotion quickly adapted to any new frequency tested and the reversibility of the adaptation was confirmed.
evidence: The Results section describes this observation.

claim: Temporal frequency-locked vasomotion was apparent in low 4° amplitude as well as in high 25° amplitude.
source: Similarly, the effect of changing the spatial amplitude of the horizontal oscillations was examined, while keeping other parameters fixed. A large amplitude would require the mouse to move its eyes largely within their eye sockets. The temporal frequency-locked vasomotion was apparent in the low 4° amplitude as well as in the high 25° amplitude (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Vasomotion was substantially induced in response to any amplitude between 4° and 25°.
source: The relative peak ratio normalized to that of 17° amplitude showed that the vasomotion was substantially induced in response to any amplitude between 4° and 25° (Figure 5D, middle panel).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Vasomotion could follow visual stimuli irrespective of the fineness of the presented stripes.
source: Lastly, the horizontal spatial cycle of the vertical stripes was varied (Figure 5C). Again, the vasomotion could follow the visual stimuli irrespective of the fineness of the presented stripes (Figure 5D, right panel).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The eye tracked visual stimulation well with virtually no phase shift relative to the visual stimulation cycle.
source: First, the right eye trace in response to the horizontally oscillating visual stimulus was examined (Figure 6A). The eye tracked the visual stimulation well and there was virtually no phase shift in the eye trace relative to the visual stimulation cycle (Figure 6B).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The phase of TexasRed signal in the flocculus was either 0° or 180° relative to visual stimulation, depending on the animal.
source: The TexasRed signal fluctuation in the flocculus in the right hemisphere was oscillatory with the visual stimulation; however, the phase of the TexasRed signal was either 0° or 180° relative to the visual stimulation, depending on the animal (Figure 6C).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Maximum vasodilation and vasoconstriction occur when the speed of eye movement reaches zero.
source: In either mouse, the maximum vasodilation and vasoconstriction occur when the speed of the eye movement reaches zero.
evidence: The Results section infers this from the phase relationship.

claim: Under anesthesia with isoflurane, eye movement was not induced and dYFP signal did not oscillate.
source: To address this possibility, the mouse was anesthetized by isoflurane (Figure 6D). Under anesthesia, the eye fails to follow the screen. The vasomotion was detected with the 'shadow' imaging method by studying the dYFP fluctuations. No oscillatory signals were detected in the dYFP.
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Visual stimulus on the presented screen does not reach the optical fiber to directly induce oscillatory signals.
source: Next, in the TexasRed injected mouse, the HOKR visual stimulation was presented, which induced a nice eye movement following the visual stimulus (Figure 6E). However, in this case, we did not send the excitation light through the optical fiber but kept the PMT active. If the visual stimulus on the presented screen is somehow reaching the optical fiber, then it should be detected in this condition, but it was not.
evidence: The Results section describes control experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The cycle of visual stimulation producing either a large or small eye movement did not always result in a large or small amplitude fluctuation of vasomotion, respectively.
source: The amplitude of the oscillatory eye movement was plotted against the PR0.25 of the TexasRed during a single visual session (Figure 6G). The cycle of visual stimulation producing either a large or small eye movement did not always result in a large or small amplitude fluctuation of the vasomotion, respectively, and no correlation was found.
evidence: The Results section describes analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: No correlation was found between eye movement amplitude and PR0.25 of TexasRed.
source: The amplitude of the oscillatory eye movement was plotted against the PR0.25 of the TexasRed during a single visual session (Figure 6G). The cycle of visual stimulation producing either a large or small eye movement did not always result in a large or small amplitude fluctuation of the vasomotion, respectively, and no correlation was found.
evidence: The Results section describes statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Repeated HOKR training results in larger amplitude of eye oscillations, reaching close to the actual visual presentation amplitude.
source: Repeated HOKR training usually results in a larger amplitude of the eye oscillations, which reaches close to the actual visual presentation amplitude.
evidence: The Results section states this as established knowledge.

claim: HOKR performance increase relies on neuronal and glial activity in the cerebellar flocculus.
source: It has been shown that HOKR performance increase relies on the neuronal and glial activity in the cerebellar flocculus (Kanaya et al., 2023).
evidence: The Results section cites a source supporting this mechanism.

claim: HOKR performance increased with repeated training sessions during day 1.
source: As described previously, HOKR performance increased with repeated training sessions during day 1 (Figure 7B-D).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: PR0.25 of autofluorescence signal changes with spaced training protocol basically followed plastic changes of eye movement.
source: The PR0.25 of the autofluorescence signal changes with the spaced training protocol basically followed the plastic changes of the eye movement (Figure 7E).
evidence: The Results section describes observations shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A strong correlation was found between average HOKR relative gains and average PR0.25 values across 10 tests.
source: The average HOKR relative gains were plotted against the average PR0.25 values and a strong correlation was found (Figure 7F; each data point represents an average score of n = 15 mice and 10 data points are shown for the 10 tests).
evidence: The Results section describes correlation analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A large variance was found both in HOKR relative gain and PR0.25 of autofluorescence fluctuations across animals.
source: In addition, it should be pointed out that a large variance was found both in the HOKR relative gain and the PR0.25 of the autofluorescence fluctuations across animals (X and Y error bars indicate S.D. in Figure 7F).
evidence: The Results section describes the variance shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A moderate but significant correlation was found between HOKR relative gain on day 5 normalized to fourth training on day 1 and PR0.25 of autofluorescence fluctuations during last 5 min of fourth training session on day 1.
source: HOKR relative gain on day 5 normalized to that for the fourth training on day 1 was plotted against the PR0.25 of the autofluorescence fluctuations during the last 5 min of the fourth training session on day 1 (Figure 7G). Interestingly, a moderate but significant correlation between these parameters was found (n = 15 mice).
evidence: The Results section describes correlation analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The level of visually induced vasomotion may contribute to the consolidation of HOKR performance in later days.
source: This may suggest that the level of visually induced vasomotion contributes to the consolidation of HOKR performance in later days.
evidence: The Results section proposes this interpretation of the correlation.

claim: There is a complex and intimate relationship between vasomotion and neuronal circuit plasticity, learning, and memory.
source: These results imply a complex and intimate relationship between vasomotion and neuronal circuit plasticity, learning, and memory.
evidence: The Results section concludes this from the correlation findings.

claim: The initial drive for vasomotion or sensory-evoked hyperemia must be coming from neuronal activity in the visual system.
source: The initial drive for the vasomotion, or the sensory-evoked hyperemia, must be coming from the neuronal activity in the visual system.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this mechanism.

claim: Visually induced vasomotion is likely triggered by activation of neurovascular interaction.
source: The visually induced vasomotion is likely triggered by activation of the neurovascular interaction (Kayser et al., 2004; van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claim: The global entrainment could be realized through separate mechanisms from local neurovascular coupling.
source: The global entrainment could be realized through separate mechanisms from the local neurovascular coupling.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claim: Repeated visual stimulus may induce synaptic plasticity at neuronal projections from retina to a central nucleus that controls brain-wide vasomotion, such as in the autonomic nerve system.
source: Repeated visual stimulus may induce synaptic plasticity not in the visual system but at the neuronal projections from the retina to a central nucleus that controls a brain-wide vasomotion, such as in the autonomic nerve system (Korte et al., 2023).
evidence: The Discussion proposes this mechanism with citation.

claim: Neurovascular coupling could be enhanced with increased responsiveness of vascules and vascular-to-vascular coupling could also be potentiated.
source: Instead, the neurovascular coupling could be enhanced with increased responsiveness of the vascules and vascular-to-vascular coupling could also be potentiated.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this alternative mechanism.

claim: Glucose and oxygen are likely to be abundantly delivered during vasodilation phase compared to vasoconstriction phase of vasomotion.
source: Glucose and oxygen are likely to be abundantly delivered during the vasodilation phase compared to the vasoconstriction phase of vasomotion.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this based on physiological reasoning.

claim: Concentration fluctuation of metabolites such as NADH, NADPH, and FAD could lag in time to changes in blood flow.
source: These molecules will trigger cell metabolism and endogenous fluorescent molecules such as NADH, NADPH, and FAD may increase or decrease with a certain delay. These molecules are required for biochemical reactions to occur. Therefore, the concentration fluctuation of these metabolites could lag in time to the changes in the blood flow.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this explanation for the phase shift.

claim: Stress induced by tail-vein injection could not interfere with the generation of visually induced vasomotion.
source: Before session 4, TexasRed was injected again to visualize the vasomotion. The oscillatory vasomotion was clearly observed in session 4, indicating that the stress induced by tail-vein injection could not interfere with the generation of visually induced vasomotion.
evidence: The Discussion concludes this from the experimental observations.

claim: It is not possible to distinguish whether visually induced oscillatory vasomotion was driven by mechanisms of spontaneous vasomotion or functional hyperemia.
source: It is not possible to distinguish whether the visually induced oscillatory vasomotion observed in this study was driven by the mechanisms of spontaneous vasomotion or functional hyperemia.
evidence: The Discussion acknowledges this limitation.

claim: Spontaneous vasomotion requires coordinated activity of vascular SMCs.
source: The spontaneous vasomotion requires the coordinated activity of the vascular SMCs.
evidence: The Discussion states this as established knowledge.

claim: Oscillatory release of calcium ions from sarcoplasmic reticulum results in oscillations in membrane potential of SMCs.
source: Oscillatory release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum results in oscillations in the membrane potential of SMCs. Via the gap junctions between SMCs, synchronized oscillations are created (Haddock et al., 2006; Haddock and Hill, 2002; Hill et al., 1999; Peng et al., 2001; Schuster et al., 2001).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claim: Blood flow in the central nervous system was assumed to be regulated primarily by SMCs in precapillary arterioles.
source: Blood flow in the central nervous system was assumed to be regulated primarily by the SMCs in precapillary arterioles; however, capillaries lacking smooth muscle have been shown to be controlled by pericytes (Peppiatt et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this knowledge.

claim: Capillaries lacking smooth muscle have been shown to be controlled by pericytes.
source: Blood flow in the central nervous system was assumed to be regulated primarily by the SMCs in precapillary arterioles; however, capillaries lacking smooth muscle have been shown to be controlled by pericytes (Peppiatt et al., 2006).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this finding.

claim: Whether astrocytic calcium is involved in controlling local cerebral blood flow is in question.
source: Astrocytes also constitute the neurovascular unit; however, whether astrocytic calcium is involved in controlling local cerebral blood flow is in question (Ozawa et al., 2023).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source questioning this mechanism.

claim: Astrocytes could regulate vasomotor amplitudes via stretch-mediated feedback.
source: It is still possible that astrocytes could regulate vasomotor amplitudes via stretch-mediated feedback (Bazargani and Attwell, 2016; Haidey et al., 2021).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this possibility.

claim: Spontaneous vasomotion has been suggested to be driven by periodic neural activity in the resting state.
source: Spontaneous vasomotion has been suggested to be driven by the periodic neural activity in the resting state (Martuzzi et al., 2009; Mateo et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this mechanism.

claim: Neuronal projections from neuronal nuclei projecting to the whole brain may be controlling and synchronizing vasomotion via neurovascular coupling.
source: Neuronal projections from the neuronal nuclei projecting to the whole brain may be controlling and synchronizing vasomotion via neurovascular coupling (Korte et al., 2023).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this possibility.

claim: Ultra-slow vasomotion could be driven not only by neuronal rhythms but also by oscillatory systemic changes, such as blood pressure and carbon dioxide in the blood.
source: It is also possible that ultra-slow vasomotion could be driven not only by the neuronal rhythms but also by the oscillatory systemic changes, such as blood pressure and carbon dioxide in the blood (Panerai et al., 1998; Sassaroli et al., 2012; Wise et al., 2004).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this possibility.

claim: Functional hyperemia has been shown to be induced by visual stimulation.
source: Functional hyperemia has been shown to be induced by visual stimulation (Heeger et al., 2000; Kayser et al., 2004; Niessing et al., 2005; Rivadulla et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2021; Stickland et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this phenomenon.

claim: If a pulsatile visual stimulus is periodically presented, that would result in vasomotion fluctuation with the same frequency as the presented visual stimulus.
source: If a pulsatile visual stimulus is periodically presented, that would result in vasomotion fluctuation with the same frequency as the presented visual stimulus (Kayser et al., 2004; van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this relationship.

claim: Previously, visual stimulus-evoked vasomotion was reported to be restricted to the visual cortex.
source: Previously, such visual stimulus-evoked vasomotion was reported to be restricted to the visual cortex (van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source reporting this finding.

claim: Vasomotion entrainment may be induced in other areas as well, including the limbic system and the brain stem.
source: It is possible that vasomotion entrainment is induced in other areas as well, including the limbic system and the brain stem.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claim: Mathematical modeling has shown that effective vascular resistance decreases with vasomotion.
source: Mathematical modeling has shown that effective vascular resistance decreases with vasomotion (Meyer et al., 2002).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this finding.

claim: Low-frequency vasomotion has been shown to be beneficial for tissue oxygenation, especially in regions where perfusion is restricted.
source: Low-frequency vasomotion has been shown to be beneficial for tissue oxygenation, especially in regions where perfusion is restricted (Davis et al., 2008; Nilsson and Aalkjaer, 2003).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this benefit.

claim: Vasomotion could drive paravascular clearance or intramural periarterial drainage (IPAD).
source: Furthermore, it was recently reported that vasomotion could also drive paravascular clearance or intramural periarterial drainage (IPAD) (van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this function.

claim: Simulation modeling suggested that vasomotion was required for efficient IPAD.
source: Initially, arterial pulsation from the heart was considered to be the driving force for the IPAD; however, simulation modeling suggested that vasomotion was required for the efficient IPAD (Aldea et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this modeling result.

claim: 40 Hz sensory stimulation has been proposed to be potentially beneficial for treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
source: 40 Hz sensory stimulation has been proposed to be potentially beneficial for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Adaikkan et al., 2019; Iaccarino et al., 2016; Martorell et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this proposal.

claim: It was recently claimed that 40 Hz flickering light does not entrain gamma oscillations and suppress amyloid beta accumulation in brains of AD model mouse.
source: However, it was recently claimed that the 40 Hz flickering light does not entrain gamma oscillations and suppress amyloid beta (Aβ) accumulation in the brains of the AD model mouse (Soula et al., 2023).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source contradicting the previous claim.

claim: Flashing visual stimuli could increase the amplitude of vasomotion, which resulted in an increase in paravascular clearance rates in visual cortex of awake mice.
source: In another study, it was shown that flashing visual stimuli could increase the amplitude of vasomotion, which resulted in an increase in the paravascular clearance rates in the visual cortex of awake mice (van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this finding.

claim: In mice with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, impaired paravascular clearance and Aβ accumulation occur.
source: In mice with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, impaired paravascular clearance and Aβ accumulation occur (Charidimou et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2016).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting this finding.

claim: Low-frequency arteriolar oscillations could drive the drainage of soluble waste products.
source: It was also suggested that low-frequency arteriolar oscillations could drive the drainage of soluble waste products (van Veluw et al., 2020).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this suggestion.

claim: HOKR-driving oscillatory visual stimulus at 0.25 Hz is effective in producing brain-wide oscillatory vasomotion.
source: In our study, we show that the HOKR-driving oscillatory visual stimulus, which is much slower (0.25 Hz) than the 40 Hz, is effective in producing a brain-wide oscillatory vasomotion.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's findings.

claim: Repeated presentation with spaced training protocol was effective in driving plastic vasomotion entrainment.
source: In addition, repeated presentation with the spaced training protocol was effective in driving the plastic vasomotion entrainment.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's findings.

claim: Paravascular clearance and drainage of waste products, such as Aβ, may be enhanced with vasomotion entrainment.
source: Paravascular clearance and drainage of waste products, such as Aβ, may be enhanced with vasomotion entrainment.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claim: Synaptic plasticity change related to cerebellar motor learning is enhanced in parallel with vasomotion entrainment.
source: We show that synaptic plasticity change related to cerebellar motor learning is enhanced in parallel with the vasomotion entrainment.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the study's findings.

claim: Vasomotion enhancement may increase meta-plasticity and provide a basis for efficient neuronal plasticity to occur.
source: It is possible that vasomotion enhancement may increase the meta-plasticity and provide a basis for efficient neuronal plasticity to occur.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claim: Neuron-to-astrocyte signaling pathways have been identified in the cerebellum.
source: In the cerebellum, neuron-to-astrocyte (or Bergmann glia) (Matsui et al., 2005; Matsui and Jahr, 2004; Matsui and Jahr, 2003) and astrocyte-to-neuron (Beppu et al., 2021; Beppu et al., 2014; Sasaki et al., 2012) signaling pathways have been identified and such neuron-astrocyte interaction has been shown to be essential for the online HOKR learning to occur (Kanaya et al., 2023).
evidence: The Discussion cites sources supporting these signaling pathways.

claim: Neuron-astrocyte interaction has been shown to be essential for online HOKR learning to occur.
source: In the cerebellum, neuron-to-astrocyte (or Bergmann glia) (Matsui et al., 2005; Matsui and Jahr, 2004; Matsui and Jahr, 2003) and astrocyte-to-neuron (Beppu et al., 2021; Beppu et al., 2014; Sasaki et al., 2012) signaling pathways have been identified and such neuron-astrocyte interaction has been shown to be essential for the online HOKR learning to occur (Kanaya et al., 2023).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this requirement.

claim: Late offline HOKR learning was dependent in part on the phagocytosis activity of astrocytes.
source: Late offline HOKR learning was dependent in part on the phagocytosis activity of astrocytes (Morizawa et al., 2022).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this mechanism.

claim: Energy required for long-term plastic changes in the brain may be supported by cooperative actions of astrocytes and entrained vasomotion.
source: It is possible that the energy required for the long-term plastic changes in the brain is supported by the cooperative actions of the astrocytes and the entrained vasomotion.
evidence: The Discussion proposes this possibility.

claim: Aβ has been shown to constrict capillaries and the resulting slight hypoxia and neuronal damage may be the cause of dementia in AD.
source: Aβ has been shown to constrict capillaries and the resulting slight hypoxia and neuronal damage may actually be the cause of dementia in AD (Nortley et al., 2019).
evidence: The Discussion cites a source supporting this mechanism.

claim: C57BL/6NJcl male mice (2–4 months old) were used to reduce variance of HOKR performance among animals.
source: C57BL/6NJcl male mice (2–4 months old) were used in this study in order to reduce the variance of HOKR performance among animals (Aziz et al., 2014).
evidence: The Materials and methods section explains the rationale for mouse selection with citation.
